University of Rhode Island Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses Online courses can and should use a wide variety of assessment methods, which should be designed to promote academic integrity.
In some disciplines proctored exams provide a useful tool for assessment of student learning in online courses.
When designing an online course, faculty should carefully balance the potential difficulties and costs for students who are unable to come to campus at a specific time for testing (i.e. working adults, students who live out of state, Faculty must provide clear guidance to students if they require a proctored exam.
The faculty member must state in their syllabus the beginning of the semester, if a proctored exam is required for the course.
They must note that the exam will be offered during one of the common exam times.
They must alert students as soon as possible: · The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered at the Kingston and/or Providence campuses.
The scheduled window period in which the exam is to be completed by those students who cannot come to campus and should include a link to the URI resources concerning proctored exams.

Scheduling Proctored Exams for Online Classes: ·Proctored final exams for online classes must be scheduled according to the appropriate policies of the campus where the course is offered (Kingston or Providence).
As soon as the exam is scheduled, faculty should make students aware of the time and date, and place It is the instructor's responsibility to ensure proper proctoring of the on campus exam.
Acceptable Exam Proctors outside of URI Students who cannot come to campus are responsible for making alternative arrangements for taking an exam by locating an acceptable proctor and location.
Proctors may not be friends or family members.
Acceptable proctors include: · Dean, academic department head, or official testing administrator of an accredited college or university Head librarian at a public library or a librarian with faculty status at an academic library ·Personnel at an exam testing center (such as ETS) Commanding officer at a military learning center Organizations that proctor have their own policies and exam takers need to be aware of these policies before taking the exam.

If there is a cost associated with an external proctored site, it is the responsibility of the student to pay that cost.
Approving a Proctor Form to the course instructor three weeks prior to the exam date.

University of Rhode Island Recommended Proctored Exam Procedure for Students If your instructor requires a proctored exam for your online course, it will be clearly noted in your syllabus on the first day of class.
You should carefully read your syllabus to understand the instructor's policy on arranging and completing a proctored exam.
Because online exams are offered in a "common exam space," the syllabus may not inclnde the exact day and time.
The instructor will provide that information to you at least four weeks before the exam is scheduled, sooner if possible.
As soon as possible, the instructor will inform you of: The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered, and which campus (Kingston or Providence).
OR if you are unable to come to campus: · The scheduled window period in which the exam is to be completed.
Finding an Exam Proctor if unable to come to URI campus Proctors may not be friends or family members.

Acceptable proctors include: · Dean, academic department head, or official testing administrator of an accredited college or university · Head librarian at an academic or public library ·Personnel at an exam testing center (such as ETS) · Commanding officer at a military learning center If there is a cost associated with an external proctored site, it is the responsibility of the student to pay that cost.
Getting a Proctor Approved After making arrangements with a proctor, the student must submit a Proctored Exam Request Form to the course instructor three weeks prior to the exam date.
Instructors will approve the arranged location and proctor, and confirm your contact with the proctor via email, telephone, or mail.
An instructor has the right not to approve a proctoring site, but will give you notice and a clear explanation so that you have the time and information to locate another proctor.
On the Day of the Exam You should meet your proctor at the agreed upon day, time and place.
You may bring with you any materials that the instructor has permitted or required for the exam (E.g.
Calculator, pencils, scratch paper, laptop). 1/10/2013 TAAC Report 2023-2024-01 Appendix A | Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-03 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual (Constitution of theFaculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and special committees as it deems necessaryto carry out its functions.
During AY 2023-2024, the University community faced operational changes,including various administrative policy initiatives and the planned transition to a new budget model, thatstressed the ability of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee to respond appropriately and react in atimely fashion.
The FSEC has agreed that creating a special committee to advise the FSEC in these andrelated matters would improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Faculty Senate.
This new groupcould assist in analyzing and making recommendations regarding any major operational changesemerging under the university strategic plan or under independent leadership of the President, VicePresidents, or Deans; including new budget models and their implementations; and any other specificoperational expenditures relevant to faculty.

Motion: to approve the creation of a Special Budget and Administration Committee to remain in effectuntil the end of Academic Year 2025-2026.
The Committee shall provide reports on their activities to theFaculty Senate at least annually and more often as directed by the FSEC or the Senate.
Any specificproposals for action will flow from the Special Committee to the FSEC and then to the Senate.
Activitiesof the Special Committee will include but not be limited to: review and if necessary develop measuresfor tracking major or incremental expenditures, with the aim of ensuring balanced support of facultyinterests; request information on the university’s performance toward any new goals set up under thenew incentive-based budget model (IBB) and raise questions about the correspondence of theseallocations against performance metrics (KPIs); monitor directions of administrative policies with the aimof supporting academic freedom and faculty efforts.

The new Special Committee shall makerecommendations to the executive committee and the senate about formal responses to: any plans orproposals by the committees and individuals tasked with the implementation and functioning of theincentive-based budget model; any positions or policy initiatives of the institutional research office,administrative policy groups, purchasing, capital projects, and similar groups as they may be identified orarise.
They may also engage in advocacy on behalf of the faculty for support of research, instruction,professional development, travel, course caps, and service time, so that faculty thrive in their workunder their contractual roles.
Membership will be three senators and 2 non senators, and the chair will be elected by the committeefollowing input from the senate executive committee.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-04 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual(Constitution of the Faculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and specialcommittees as it deems necessary to carry out its functions.
The Executive Committee wasapproached by the Provost’s office regarding the need for more robust ongoing assessment andcontinuous improvement of the General Education Program.
They suggested the formation of a“steering committee” to recommend best practices for assessing the overall program and to helpdetermine if the current program is achieving the goals and outcomes envisioned in the enablinglegislation.
The FSEC and the General Education Committee (GEC) have worked on thisextensively this year and considered a variety of alternatives, including reconstituting theexisting standing committee and creating a new permanent joint committee.

FSEC ultimatelyagreed that creating a time-limited, special committee would be most effective at this stage.Other recommendations for future action can flow from this working group depending on theiranalysis and findings.
MOTION: to approve the creation of a Special Committee to serve in an advisory capacity to theGEC in the fulfillment of its duties related to the evaluation of the General Education Program:the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation.
GEC shall be responsible for designing specific tasks for the special committee to address overthe course of the 2024-2025 academic year and for making decisions relating to the membershipof the committee and securing commitments from faculty (and any other stakeholders deemedappropriate and advisable) to serve on the special committee by September 12, 2024 (Senateorientation meeting).
GEC shall report to the FS on the membership and planned tasks for the Special AdvisoryCommittee on General Education Program Evaluation at the September 19, 2024 meeting of theFaculty Senate.

GEC shall make recommendations to the FS regarding the advisability ofcontinuing the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation orconstituting a permanent committee at the April 2025 Faculty Senate meeting.

Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-02 Resolution to Recognize Professors Tyler and Killilea for Exceptional Service as University Ombuds Whereas, Professors Gerry Tyler and Al Killilea have served the University of Rhode Island with unparalleled dedication and integrity since their appointments as Ombuds in 2013; and Whereas, their service has been marked by a Herculean effort and Socratic wisdom, embodying the highest ideals of diplomacy and fairness in the handling of complex and sensitive issues; and Whereas, despite the challenges of limited resources and vast institutional needs, Gerry and Al have distinguished their tenures through a steadfast commitment to justice and equity, providing immeasurable support to faculty, graduate students, undergraduate students, and staff; and Whereas, they have maintained a commendable partnership characterized by mutual respect and camaraderie, contributing significantly to the improvement of our university’s academic and administrative environment; and Whereas, their unique ability to navigate the intricacies of academia with minimal fanfare and maximal impact has set a precedent that enriches our community’s cultural and ethical landscape; and Whereas, this year marks a notable first in the history of the University of Rhode Island in recognizing two distinguished colleagues simultaneously with a single resolution for their exceptional contributions as University Ombuds; Now, therefore, be it resolved that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island hereby expresses its deepest gratitude and appreciation to Professors Tyler and Killilea for their exceptional service and contributions to our community; Be it further resolved that this resolution be entered into the official records of the Faculty Senate and a copy thereof be presented to each of the honorees in recognition of their significant and enduring contributions to the University of Rhode Island.

CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

We are at a unique moment in our history where long-standing struggles of racism, gender inequality, LGBTQ+, socio-economic status, ability, and religious differences are intensified and up for debate in the public and private spheres.
Knowing more about the root causes of the struggles LGBTQ+ individuals experience in the areas of employment, housing, politics, immigration controls, and legal institutions, to name a few, creates an opening for students to engage in systemic change and re-think their lived experiences.
The purpose of this minor is to expose students to histories, theories, concepts, and methods that have contested historical and ongoing harm and oppression.
Students are encouraged to examine their social location, lived experiences, collaborative engagement, and organizing capacity to transform our world by learning how societal structures keep inequality and oppression alive.
The QTS Minor will offer students, especially younger generations, an opportunity to read, discuss, and engage with transnational issues that affect the lives of queer and transgender communities.

Since we live in a transnational world, the QTS minor will allow students to read, think, and analyze social justice issues through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework.
While the QTS is complementary and overlaps with courses in the GWS, this minor offers an advanced level of proficiency in Queer and Transgender studies, politics, and culture, with a social justice commitment to scholarship, community engagement, and global citizenship.
From participating in interdisciplinary and innovative research, to social activism, to policy work in housing, wage gap, mental and medical services, media coverage, and decriminalization, these are some of the issues in which students will gain exposure, knowledge, and practical experiences to the problems affecting queer and transgender communities.
By broadening the scope of the QTS minor through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework, students will be able to expand their prospects in the job market.
URI is “one of the top 50 LGBTQ-friendly universities in the nation.” A minor in Queer and Transgender Studies will add to the university’s local and international reputation as a leader for LGBTQ+ students.

While the university and the center for Gender and Sexuality pride themselves on education, support, and engagement for LGBTQ+, no sustained intellectual program caters to students’ needs to study queer and transgender histories.
This minor will fill this educational gap and change the campus community’s climate.
For instance, studies have shown that an increasing number of U.S. adults consider themselves LGBTQ+, with Gen Z representing the large segment of LGBTQ+.
Gallup Poll, Social Services report indicated that at least 54.6% of LGBT Americans identify as bisexual, with Generation Z (1997-2002) representing 15.9% of the U.S. population. [1] The University of Rhode Island Climate Survey indicates that 730 students identify as LGBTQ+, roughly 18.3% of the 4,555 students surveyed.
The minor will attract not only this demographic but offer existing students at URI an intellectual space to explore their lived experiences.

While a growing younger American population identifies or has some experience with same-sex attractions, in 2022, more than 200 anti-LGBT bills were introduced in several states across the U.S. [2] These contradictions reveal a discord between public needs and opponents who continue to push anti-LGBTQ+ legislation.
However, this is not only a U.S.-based issue; similar trends of backlash against LGBTQ+ minorities are occurring in Brazil, Ghana, Russia, and Hungary.
For instance, the Florida "Don't Say Gay" bill was modeled after Hungarian anti-LGBTQ+ bills. [3] There is a global shift towards authoritarianism which seeks to threaten years of marginal gains made by minorities across race, class, gender, sexual, ability, and ethnicity.
The social, political, and economic gains and rights acquired over the last 60 years are subjected to state and national interventions, with growing concerns that minority rights will be rescinded.
Despite the LGBTQ+ population being more visible than ever, there is still systematic discrimination and oppression across post-secondary institutions, civil services, the military, employment, and health care, to name a few.

Queer and Trans Disability Studies: This seminar introduces the key concepts and contentions of disability studies and the disability justice movement through its queer and trans activists and thinkers.

Through theoretical texts, novels, personal narratives, and art created by queer and trans disabled people, we will explore the ways that disabled people are challenging systemic ableism: the devaluing of disabled lives and experiences, disabling structures and systems, and the privileging of normative ways of being.

Using “queer intimacy” as a heuristic analytic device, we will explore how feelings, emotions, affects, and textures allow us to position intimacy in relation to broader intersectional categories of race, gender, sexuality, nation, and class. ‘Queer Intimacy’ attends to practices that spill out, over, and beyond �xed subjective identities and social, political, and economic structures.

Queer and Feminist Methods: Research methodologies and methods are foundational in advancing our knowledge of the world.
Yet, theories and methods are also domination, power, and control tools.
This interdisciplinary seminar examines non-normative research methodologies as a lens to disrupt dominant knowledge production in the West, centering theories, ideas, and methods from alternative perspectives.
